title: Truce begins in Ukraine city where residents ate weeds to survive
description: A truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where residents have been trapped without food, water and electricity.Ukrainian o
body: A truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where residents have been trapped without food, water and electricity.Ukrainian officials and Russia's defence ministry say the limited ceasefire is being respected. The truce, which the White House said was secured by US First Lady Melania Trump, is meant to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuation on Friday. Oleshky, along the front line in the Kherson region, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and on the other by Russian forces.Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.Many worry the truce will not hold, with one resident saying: "I don't believe in Russia's humanity."Oleshky, home to 24,000 people before the war, was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Ukraine now estimates some 6,000 people, including 200 children, remain in the city and its surrounding areas.No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water for three years.Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies but has not had success in recent months, and it is deemed too dangerous to risk leaving on foot along mined roads out of the city. The ceasefire is supposed to allow supplies to reach the city and enable its roads to be cleared of mines to allow people safe passage out.One woman told the BBC she is in hospital recovering from two surgeries after stepping on a land mine."I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join Friday's planned evacuation.It is hard to make contact with people in Oleshky as communication is patchy and and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians, making it is difficult to verify reports the ceasefire is being implemented.Many details on the evacuations plans are unclear, initially including how and where to register for it. Some people want to know if they can bring their pets. Others are questioning what future they will have if they opt to leave their homes.While people are optimistic about leaving, there are also fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could see them be taken away and tortured. Someone who has been speaking to family in Oleshky said they fear shooting could restart during evacuations and Ukraine will somehow be blamed for not upholding the truce.Last month, the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.In response to the situation, the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire, with no details for how long it would last.Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram it had stopped firing toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson - across the river from Oleshky - at 04:00 Moscow time (01:00 GMT) in preparation for the humanitarian operation.Ukraine's parliament commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, also confirmed in a social media post that the ceasefire had begun."As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.The White House said in the statement last week that "non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require".While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.In August 2025, she penned a letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".While a truce is under way in Oleshky, elsewhere strikes continue. On Monday evening, attacks on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv hit a university and a bridge, killing one person and injuring 14 others.In Russia, one person was killed and six others were injured after a Ukrainian drone strike on Bryansk.Additional reporting by Hafsa Khalil and Sareen Habeshian

schema.headline: Truce begins in Ukraine city where residents ate weeds to survive

title: Anthropic warns of AI's 'catastrophic risks' ahead of major IPO
description: Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blo
body: Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn. Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance"."In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI. Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields."We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.

schema.headline: Anthropic warns of AI's 'catastrophic risks' ahead of major IPO

title: Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America
description: "Brazil will not accept being anyone's backyard," Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva declared in his election victory speech, a me
body: "Brazil will not accept being anyone's backyard," Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva declared in his election victory speech, a message squarely aimed at Washington.Domestic elections are rarely won on foreign policy, and this one was no different. But Lula's defiance against what he has described as US interference in Brazilian affairs evoked a patriotic spirit that proved an effective campaigning tool.It also chimed with his wider brand of politics as a former union leader: standing up to powerful figures.Paradoxically, it seems to have earned him President Donald Trump's respect. "I like Lula, we get along well," Trump said, responding to the result. "I didn't take sides," he added, before calling the election "terrible" and "rigged".If that sounds muddled, it is because the relationship between the two men is not straightforward. Trump did not explicitly endorse Lula's rival Flávio Bolsonaro, who refused to recognise the result. But Trump was a close ally of Flávio's father, the former President Jair Bolsonaro.When I spoke to Lula at his residence about a year ago, relations had hit rock bottom. He told me he had "no relationship" with Trump, that they had never spoken, and that he had no intention of picking up the phone. Trump had recently imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, largely as a political response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which the US president called a "witch-hunt".Rather than tiptoeing around Trump, as some US allies did, Lula fought back – and it paid off. He made fiery speeches invoking Brazilian sovereignty, attacked US interference in the judicial process, and took to wearing a blue cap reading "Brazil belongs to Brazilians". His approval ratings jumped. He accused the Bolsonaro family, who had lobbied for the tariffs, of being unpatriotic – a blow to a political right that so often claims patriotism as its terrain. Even some in the agricultural lobby, typically strong Bolsonaro supporters but reliant on US trade, thought Lula had a point.The US eventually backed down and reduced the tariffs, although they have since risen again. Relations then improved. The two men spoke at the United Nations and later met in the Oval Office, where Trump called the talks "very good" and Lula said he left "very satisfied". Another indication, perhaps, that Trump likes a strong leader.So why might Trump be unhappy with the result?Latin America has swung to the right, with Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, Argentina and Peru all electing presidents closely aligned with the Trump administration. Trump has sought to use these allies to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere, a strategy he has dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine".Christopher Sabatini, senior fellow for Latin America at Chatham House, notes that Trump thought Brazil would be the "10th and biggest prize" after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round. Brazil is Latin America's largest economy, and the younger Bolsonaro was expected to join Trump's "Shield of Americas" coalition against narco-trafficking. Brazil also holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals after China, and the US had been eyeing preferential access.The relationship has thawed, but with four more years ahead for Lula, several issues could reignite tensions.Brazil accused the US earlier this year of trying to cast doubt on its electoral system and denied visas to two state department officials planning to visit. The US called this "baseless" and revoked the Brazilian ambassador's visa in response. If Trump keeps calling this result "rigged", further diplomatic fallout is likely.Lula has also vehemently opposed US military action in the region, from the seizure of Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela to the bombing of alleged drug-trafficking vessels. He lambasted Washington for designating Brazil's two major gangs as terrorist organisations after lobbying from Flávio Bolsonaro, and warned of attacks on Brazilian sovereignty.It is a sensitive subject for a political left that remembers the region's brutal 20th Century dictatorships, many backed by the CIA in the name of stopping communism.Then there is US tech. Lula's campaign accused Meta of favouring Flávio Bolsonaro. Meta denied this but admitted moderation issues and technical errors had wrongly removed some posts or limited their reach. Lula's supporters responded by sharing his messages through a 10-million-strong WhatsApp group to bypass the algorithms.Separately, the Trump administration is unhappy with Pix, Brazil's instant payment system, which has boosted the economy, but which the US sees as taking business from Visa and Mastercard.The relationship has exposed political divisions. In the campaign, Bolsonaro supporters waved US flags at their rallies and, in one case, an inflatable saying "Trump Nuke Brazil", while Lula and his supporters accused Flávio Bolsonaro of protecting US interests over Brazil's.Still, tensions can be overstated.The US remains Brazil's second-biggest trading partner after China, and for now the two leaders get on. Whether that lasts will depend on how far the US tries to intervene in Brazilian affairs, and how bullish Lula is in response.

schema.headline: Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America

title: Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement
description: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movementFigure caption, Watch: Joy and disbelief on Serbian str
body: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movementFigure caption, Watch: Joy and disbelief on Serbian streets as Vučić concedes election defeatByAndré Rhoden-PaulJaroslav Lukiv and Paul KirbyEurope digital editorUpdated 26 October 2026Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to a student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.Celebrations erupted as crowds descended on the centre of Belgrade, Novi Sad and other cities. The student movement was formed less than two years ago in response to a railway station disaster blamed on corruption and negligence, but fought the election with candidates from a cross-section of Serbian society."It is clear we have lost these elections," right-wing populist leader Vučić said as he conceded. With 97% of polling stations counted, Serbia's election commission said the students had won 2.25 million votes and the former ruling party 1.67 million.The students had secured 52.7% of the vote, while Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) was on 39.2%, according to its preliminary figures late on Monday morning.Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.He called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy in front of Novi Sad station which killed 16 people.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Vučić said early results made it "clear" that his party had lostThe Student List's lead candidate Ilija Srdanović told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state."He said the anti-corruption movement, which had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia, hoped to "free the country from tyranny".There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off.  "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle."During a celebration speech, Student List candidate Radomir Saicic said Serbians  had shown "no obstacle was greater than their will", Reuters reported. "No force can forever overpower a people who have decided to take their destiny into their own hands," he added.Amid scenes of people dancing in the streets Belgrade, Selena Lebovic said the result was "really fabulous"."We are all crying, and what to say. We couldn't believe that it would be so easy," she told Reuters.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An aerial photo shows the size of the celebrations by Students' List supporters at  Slavija square in BelgradeVučić made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.The centre of Novi Sad - the northern city that triggered the student-led protests - was crowded. "Everything is going to get better now," David Vasić, one of those celebrating, told BBC Serbian.The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities."This is not an ordinary election victory, this is an avalanche that has wiped out an authoritarian regime and entire political scene," said Nebojša Vladisavljević, professor of political science at the University of Belgrade.There were now two big political groups in Serbia, and the Student List had "absolute legitimacy" to govern for the coming years, he told BBC Serbian.The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.Vučić and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption.Vučić, who backed Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov praised Vučić's contribution to relations with Russia and hoped "the new political force" in Belgrade would understand that co-operation with Moscow was in Serbia's interests: "But, as you know, it takes two to tango."His defeat was welcomed by Hungary's prime minister, Péter Magyar, who said he was delighted to hear from the Student List's leaders "how much strength our victory in April had given them". Magyar's party ended 16 years of Viktor Orbán rule, while Vučić's SNS party had been in power since 2012.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Ilija Srdanović, Student List's leading candidate, pictured during celebrations late on SundayEuropean Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said "a new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together".Earlier in the day, long queues were seen outside polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia.This was also the case outside booths in a number of countries with sizeable Serbian communities - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Germany's Munich, and Los Angeles and Chicago in the US.In France, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain in Paris.The election was held amid high tensions across Serbia, with police sealing off streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) in Belgrade.Attention will now turn to who will lead the Student List as prime minister. Presidential elections are due to take place in December, with parliament speaker Ana Brnabić currently filling the role in a caretaker capacity.

schema.headline: Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement

title: Brazil election: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn race around
description: The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particu
body: The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off"."Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult. While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback. Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights."It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media."It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement."Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration."I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed."We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

schema.headline: Brazil election: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn race around

title: María Machado returns from exile to a Venezuela reshaped by Trump
description: Figure caption, Watch: Crowds welcome Venezuela's María Corina Machado after months in exileByWill GrantBBC's Mexico, Central America and Cuba corresp
body: Figure caption, Watch: Crowds welcome Venezuela's María Corina Machado after months in exileByWill GrantBBC's Mexico, Central America and Cuba correspondentDriving down roads lined with jubilant supporters from the western state of Lara to the capital Caracas, Maria Corina Machado's return to Venezuela could hardly have been more different to her exit 10 months earlier.Colourful, loud, open and defiant, it stood in stark contrast to the way the Venezuelan opposition leader slipped out of the country in the dead of night in December last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo.She had been unable to make it back to her homeland until now, thwarted on several occasions by the Venezuelan government - and by the Trump administration,  which insisted the "time wasn't right" for her return.Now, it appears, it is."Maria Corina is the indisputable leader of Venezuela," says 20-year-old Gregory Noriega, wearing a sweatshirt emblazoned with the logo of the opposition movement Vente Venezuela. "Her return represents hope."Image caption, Gregory Noriega"This is a step forward in the electoral process which we've been waiting for since last year," echoes 18-year-old Hilary, who turned out on to the streets of the capital hoping to catch a glimpse of the opposition leader on her victory lap."She's returned after the double earthquakes when Venezuela needs her," adds her friend, Manuel.  "The whole country is behind her to show that now Venezuela isn't scared." Much has changed since Machado left Venezuelan soil to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Then-President Nicolás Maduro is no longer at the top of the Venezuelan government.  Maduro was forcibly removed from power by US troops on 3 January, and whisked to New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges – to which he's pleaded not guilty. He was replaced by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has turned the page with Washington in ways few could have imagined. The bilateral relationship is today unrecognisable from the years of mutual animosity during the reigns of  President Hugo Chávez and then his handpicked successor, Maduro. The new circumstances throw up some interesting conundrums for both sides. When Machado left Venezuela, she had long been considered Washington's favoured alternative to Maduro. She returns to find the Trump administration perfectly happy with the one they've got – at least for the time being.Image source, Getty ImagesThe Trump administration recently signed a major oil deal with Venezuela which gave the US a 100-year concession over a staggering 65bn barrels of Venezuelan crude oil. The deal was reached in conjunction with a Venezuelan private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) run by a businessman with a chequered past, Alejandro Betancourt.Machado has openly criticised the deal which the Rodríguez government reached with the US, albeit careful to direct her criticism at Caracas and at Betancourt rather than President Trump, to whom she gave her peace prize and whose trust and support she craves to move forward.President Trump has repeatedly said how satisfied he is with Delcy Rodríguez, calling her "wonderful" and "a terrific person". This was the vice-president of an administration he previously described as made up of "narco-communists".But the outpouring of jubilation for Machado's caravan into the capital shows she can still count on significant support on the streets, says Venezuelan political analyst Beningno Alarcon."The return of Maria Corina Machado, in my personal view, is the most significant [political] event since 3rd January," says Alarcon. "It means the most important political leader in Venezuela is back in the country.""The reception for her return shows that her ability to mobilise her support remains intact, which means the opposition in Venezuela now has something very solid: a leadership which is present on the ground as opposed to solely in exile," he says.Alarcon provides some evidence that the opposition – and the public at large – feel more emboldened since 3 January, a situation he believes will become only more pronounced with Machado's reappearance.Image caption, Political analyst Beningno AlarconFor instance, a joint study by the political think tanks Polis and Nexo suggests that Venezuela saw three times as many street protests in the first nine months of this year as in all of 2025, with demonstrations spanning a range of issues, from politics and working conditions to water supply.Furthermore, there's evidence that the repression of such protests has reduced by more than half.In such an environment, the return of a figurehead like Machado can galvanise an electorate that has spent years fearful of the consequences of speaking out.Her return also needs to be seen within the context of the wider talks brokered by Washington between the Venezuelan government and the opposition towards a negotiated political solution. Certainly, the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, was quick to say her "safe return" to Venezuela was "the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks".The Nobel Peace Prize winner still faces charges in Venezuela ranging from treason to conspiracy of insurrection. For years, she and her supporters have dismissed the charges as politically motivated and baseless.Image caption, Young supporters of Maria MachadoHaving made at least eight attempts to return to Venezuela by air and by sea before the Trump administration gave her the green light, Machado now knows she has  Trump's blessing to be back on home soil – a position Delcy Rodríguez is both unwilling and unlikely to challenge.She called Machado's return a "show" and the entire cross-country event, which was livestreamed by her supporters over the weekend, was studiously ignored by state television outlets.But Rodríguez, too, needs a harmonious relationship with Washington if she is to avoid a fate similar to that of her predecessor and indicated she might be prepared to hold talks with Machado.For as much as Trump has complimented Rodríguez, he has also made it clear that Washington expects nothing less than her full submission and malleability on key issues like energy. Some reports have even suggested all major decision-making in the oil-rich nation is being largely dictated by Secretary Rubio via regular WhatsApp calls to the interim president.The young supporters gathered in droves in Caracas to cheer Maria Corina Machado home say their fears of criticising their government or demanding change are vanishing. Her return marked an irreversible political transition in Venezuela, they insist, one which they could barely fathom when she left for Oslo just a year ago.Figure caption, Watch:  December 2025 - BBC interview Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina MachadoAdditional reporting by Vanessa Silva in Caracas.

schema.headline: María Machado returns from exile to a Venezuela reshaped by Trump

title: Ballon d'Or predictions: Will Lamine Yamal, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe or Lionel Messi win?
description: European football expert Julien Laurens: I think he was the best player in Europe last season, especially in the Champions League where he was outstan
body: European football expert Julien Laurens: I think he was the best player in Europe last season, especially in the Champions League where he was outstanding. He helped lead the team to another title, a back-to-back one. He got the penalty in the final, scored in both semi-finals, in the quarter-final, and in the last 16. He was amazing in those huge, huge games where you want your best players to step up. He deserves to win the Ballon d'Or for being the best player in the world all the way up to the World Cup. He won't win it, unfortunately, because Lamine Yamal, for the player he is and how entertaining and spectacular he is, didn't really shine at the World Cup, even if Spain won it. He didn't really do that well in the Champions League for Barcelona, getting knocked out early. However, his style of football means he'll probably win it - but it should be Kvaratskhelia.Ex-Liverpool and Blackburn full-back Stephen Warnock: I think it will be Lamine Yamal for helping Spain to win the World Cup. If you were asking who else is in the hunt, I would say Michael Olise, but my pick personally would be Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, he is unbelievable. I love watching him play. He had such an impact for Paris St-Germain and last season he was incredible. I just don't think he will get the votes with Georgia not being in the World Cup.BBC Radio 5 Live Euro Leagues guest and Athletic reporter Rory Smith: It will probably go to Lamine Yamal because it generally goes to someone who has won the biggest trophy, and this is the World Cup. It shouldn't be him because he wasn't necessarily Spain's most important player but his fame and talent means it will be him. Personally I would give it to Kvaratskhelia. He has been the most exciting player in European club football for a while now, a valuable part of the PSG team who retained the Champions League, and crucially I think you shouldn't suffer because you come from a country who isn't in the running to win the World Cup.

schema.headline: Ballon d'Or predictions: Will Lamine Yamal, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe or Lionel Messi win?

title: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting
description: Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were rel
body: Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were released and prompted many to ask if they were making a political statement.Photos and video of the 22 October meeting show a group of bishops standing around Trump at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, one of those pictured, said he had believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity".Trump and Pope Leo XIV have a contentious relationship, and some US bishops have criticised the White House's immigration stance. Trump won the support of 55% of Catholic voters in 2024, a Pew study found.In a statement posted online, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, said the meeting was arranged by officials with the White House Faith Office to discuss issues including immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons". "In no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," Joensen said. "I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes," he added.A video of the meeting was released by Margo Martin, a special assistant to the president and communications adviser who frequently shares behind-the-scenes images of Trump on social media. Archbishop Grob said that after 90 minutes of meetings with officials, the religious leaders were ushered into the Oval Office to pray with Trump. Grob said images of the meeting later caused concern among some of his congregants. "I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he wrote."I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family have been harmed by the president's policies," he added. Grob said none of the participants in the meeting gave permission for the public distribution or posting of video or photos of the event. When contacted for comment by the BBC, the White House did not directly address questions regarding the meeting or subsequent comments by the two bishops. "There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it," White House Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement. According to Pew Research Center, which analyses religion in the US, opinions of Trump's performance have slipped among all major religious groups. In a survey this month, 30% of all US Catholics said they approved of his job performance, compared to 47% when he returned to the White House in 2025.That could have an effect on the 3 November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress. More Catholics in the survey, 42%, said they preferred the Democrats running in their local House of Representatives races, where slightly less, 39% favoured Republicans.During his second term, Trump has had a tense relationship with the head of the Catholic church, Pope Leo, as he has moved aggressively to remove people believed to be in the US illegally.Nine days before the Oval Office meeting with the bishops took place, Bishop Brendon Cahill and Walter Kim, the president of the National Association of Evangelicals, issued a statement urging "Christian compassion and wisdom in the immigration debate".They said the immigration clampdown has led to the "sowing of fear, the fracturing of families, the deprivation of due process, and the vilification of our neighbors."The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also recently condemned the Trump administration's plans to livestream a military execution, which were later scrapped.Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are Catholics who have visited the Vatican during Trump's second term.A Midwestern member of the bishops' conference, Robert Barron of Minnesota, agreed to serve on the president's Religious Liberty Commission last year, as did former New York Archbishop Timothy Dolan.

schema.headline: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting

title: Israel heads to polls for pivotal election defined by security and democracy
description: Israelis are heading to the polls for what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.Polling published on Friday suggest
body: Israelis are heading to the polls for what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.Polling published on Friday suggests incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu is in a near neck-and-neck race with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to become prime minister.But neither of their political blocs are projected to win the 61 seats needed to form a majority government - meaning weeks or months of political wrangling may lie ahead.The campaign has been shaped by the issue of security - with the opposition bloc hammering Netanyahu for the unprecedented security failure that led to the 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken back to Gaza as hostages.They have pushed for an independent commission of inquiry into the attacks - something Netanyahu has long resisted, insisting it would be biased against him.Despite the opposition's attack lines, Netanyahu has once again framed himself as "Mr Security" - pointing to what he says are strategic victories in Israel's wars across the Middle East and his close relationship with US President Donald Trump. Israel's proportional representation system means governments have always been coalitions - and the race to power can, and has, produced unexpected alliances. But this election looks especially tight - and lines in the sand have already been drawn.Eisenkot, who leads the newly formed Yashar Party, is the main figure in the so-called "change bloc", a collection of parties who have ideological differences but share the goal of ousting Netanyahu.Other leaders in the bloc include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security - and Yair Golan, a left-leaning former general.For Netanyahu, a titan of Israeli politics who first served as prime minister in 1996, a return to power will hinge on another alliance with the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties that make up his current governing coalition - the most right-wing in Israel's history.There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.Eisenkot takes a broadly similar position to Netanyahu on Gaza, and has pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through a US-led peace plan or, if necessary, military means. Israel has continued to strike Gaza almost every day since a ceasefire was agreed last year, saying it is targeting Hamas operatives. The Israeli military has killed more than 74,000 people since the start of the war, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel has faced growing international condemnation over its conduct in the war, and relations with its allies around the world have deteriorated.Eisenkot largely supports Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank - which are illegal under international law - but wants to crack down on extremist Jewish settlers whose attacks are at an all-time high, according to UN figures. He has also spoken about creating the conditions for "autonomy or a state-minus" for Palestinians - under ultimate Israeli security control.The two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - has all but disappeared from mainstream Israeli politics. Though some have speculated the Arab parties may end up informally propping up an Eisenkot-led minority government - Lieberman, a key prospective member, has ruled out being part of such an arrangement.Red lines like these mean the electoral arithmetic is complex - but it remains to be seen what kind of concessions, deals and U-turns can be reached once the results come in. An unprecedented 70,000 people have reportedly flown home from abroad to vote, while hundreds of thousands are set to cast ballots for the first time.At 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday, Israeli broadcasters will publish exit polls. These will give some indication of the direction of voting, but can vary significantly. Up and down the country, Israelis will gather to watch the results trickle in, with Netanyahu's Likud meeting in Jerusalem and Eisenkot's Yashar - formed only last year - assembling in Tel Aviv.Hundreds of thousands of Israeli soldiers and reservists will also cast ballots, but many of those votes will not begin being counted until Wednesday - meaning there may be a late boon for the right-wing parties who are thought to have strong support from that demographic.Though often framed as a run-off between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, it is possible another leader could take power, if they were to withhold their party's support for a coalition unless given the top job.An outcome dreaded by many is political deadlock - where no bloc is able to reach a majority, and a minority government cannot be formed. In that scenario, new elections would be called, with Netanyahu to remain as interim prime minister. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as parties struggled time and again to co-operate.

schema.headline: Israel heads to polls for pivotal election defined by security and democracy

title: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again
description: Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula w
body: Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old.He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s.Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism.Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement.In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history.The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform.Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system.He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation.In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities.By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor.However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education.He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - 83% - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades.Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012.Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash.Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years.Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used.He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated. In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted.Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro.When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday. Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office. And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions. His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism. Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy. His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.  Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump.The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public.The Brazilian leader told the BBC in September 2025 that he had no relationship with Trump.Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, Flávio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off.Lula accused Trump of foreign interference and said "he's not emperor of the world". But their relationship improved after a White House in May this year, after which the two leaders exchanged public compliments - Trump called Lula "dynamic", while the Brazilian president said he left the meeting "very satisfied".In July of this year, the US imposed 25% tariffs on most goods, external from Brazil.The two governments still disagree on key issues such as crime, and Lula acknowledged they are especially far apart on trade.Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".

schema.headline: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again

title: Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByBernd Debusmann Jr and Mike HillsImmigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.When he famously stepped on
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByBernd Debusmann Jr and Mike HillsImmigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since.Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts.But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress.Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency.He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both.But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far.His signature policy has played out in five key ways.1. A border that is largely closedCrossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border.His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing.When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted.By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone.On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings.To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach.That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north."President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October."The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works."2. Building of wall speeding upA vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign.Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill.According to government figures, external, about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US.Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction.Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated.Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate."Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging.Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it."I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."3. Detentions and deportations rocketingMost of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country.During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first.Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, external, a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA.But the same data, external shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%.Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office.But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 2026 that left two US citizens dead.A New York Times and Siena poll, external released on 21 October found that 50% of voters trust Democrats to handle the issue, compared with 46% for Republicans - despite the issue being a traditional Republican strength.A separate poll, from Politico and Public First, external in late September, found deep splits between Republicans on the issue, with 31% of non-MAGA Republicans, meaning those not aligned with Trump's movement, believing that campaign has become too aggressive.Figure caption, Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midterms4. Refugee intake down sharplyAfter returning to the White House last year, Trump almost immediately suspended refugee admissions, saying at the time these could only restart if they were shown to be in US interests.In February, however, an executive order signed by Trump narrowly re-opened that process for Afrikaners from South Africa, who the White House has repeatedly said are being killed and "persecuted" - a claim that the government in Pretoria has denied.The cap for refugee admissions for the 2026 fiscal year was initially set at 7,500, which was raised to 17,500 in May this year because of what the administration described as an "unforeseen emergency refugee situation".Overall refugee admissions have slowed to a relative trickle. State Department data shows that 16,292 refugees were admitted into the US in the 2026 fiscal year - of whom 16,287 were South African.By comparison, in the final two fiscal years of the Biden administration - 2023 and 2024 - 60,000 and 100,000 entered the country, respectively. In the 2024 fiscal year, the highest numbers came from Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela.Hundreds of thousands of people protected from deportation lost that protection when a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was also ended in Trump's second term. It gave vetted individuals the right to live and work in the US if their home countries were deemed to be unsafe to return to.One of those countries was Haiti. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.5. A squeeze on visas - and a $1m golden ticketOther legal pathways to come to live and work in the US have also been tightened up, through various policy changes.Dozens of countries the Trump administration has deemed a security risk have been subject to a full or partial freeze on visas and travel.Enhanced vetting and new rules that send people residing in the US back to their home countries to apply for green cards has slowed that process down.And in September 2025, a $100,000 fee on new H1-B visas for skilled workers, mostly held by Indians, stunned the US tech industry. In May this year, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X, external that registrations for 2027 were down 40%."The data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the program is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers and protecting the wages, working conditions and job opportunities of American workers," the statement added.While a court has blocked the $100,000 fee - for now - the threat of it appears to have deterred employers. But some experts have cautioned the administration's aim of protecting American jobs, raising wages and stopping firms from outsourcing may prove elusive.One study, from the Wharton School of Business, external, found that the H1-B changes would have "no significant impact" on the wages of US-born workers, with any reduction in competition offset by reduced productivity growth.Other pathways to the US have been opened, however - if you have a spare million.The "Trump Gold Card" launched in 2025 sought to entice wealthy foreigners to come live in the US in exchange for a $1m "gift" to the US government, plus a non-refundable $15,000 application fee.At the time, Trump said that the programme would boost the US economy. Its uptake, however, appears to be minimal so far. By April, only one applicant had been accepted.

schema.headline: Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US

title: October full Moon: Photos capture stunning Hunter's Moon around the world
description: Image source, Tayfun Coskun / Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, A good view for the passengers of this plane flying over San Francisco Bay in Cal
body: Image source, Tayfun Coskun / Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, A good view for the passengers of this plane flying over San Francisco Bay in California, USByJo WadeBBC Weather Published26 October 2026The October full Moon lit up skies around the world this weekend.Full Moons throughout the year have traditionally been given names that reflect what is going on in nature. This particular full moon is known by several names, including the Hunter's Moon, a name rooted in historical traditions in the Northern Hemisphere. The Hunter's Moon is known to sit in the sky for a particularly long time - similar to the preceding Harvest Moon - giving hunters extra light in the skies.Image source, BBC / BBC Weather Watcher Sam's HouseImage caption, The Hunter's Moon over Stoney Middleton in Derbyshire, UK Image source, Gary Hershorn / Getty ImagesImage caption, An autumn glow as the Hunter's Moon rises behind the skyline of midtown Manhattan in New York City, USImage source, Davide Pischettola / NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, The Moon can take on an orange or reddish hue when it is low in the sky due to the scattering of short wavelength blue light as it passes through a large depth of the atmosphere, as shown here as it rises behind the Basilica of the Madonna dei Martiri in Molfetta, ItalyImage source, BBC / BBC Weather Watcher MoxleyImage caption, A view of the moon from Kimmeridge in Dorset, UKImage source, Salih Zeki Fazlioglu / Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The full moon glowing a beautiful burnt orange over the Galata Tower in Istanbul, TurkeyImage source, BBC / BBC Weather Watcher SquizImage caption, A clear view of the Moon in Felixstowe, SuffolkImage source, Ahmad al-Rubaye / AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Moonrise in Baghdad's Firdous Square, IraqImage source, Tayfun Coskun / Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, The Hunter's Moon setting in San Francisco, California, USMore on this storyPublished11 OctoberPublished23 SeptemberPublished13 September

title: Israelis and Americans are both voting - with global consequences
description: Image source, GettyByDiplomatic correspondentReporting fromJerusalemIn the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcom
body: Image source, GettyByDiplomatic correspondentReporting fromJerusalemIn the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has highlighted his alliance with US President Donald Trump - including in this Likud party election billboard in Tel AvivMarc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC.But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and the energy that flowed through it.The Iran questionThe sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making.Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran.He has made new claims – without providing evidence – about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown.His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel.US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran.Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war.Image source, REUTERS/Jonathan ErnstImage caption, President Trump has been campaigning on behalf of Republican congressional candidates, including in Michigan on Sunday, where there's a tight Senate raceSo might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election.He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity – involving him – rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption.So real is this speculation that Netanyahu's rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has already ruled out joining any unity government. Like all mainstream Israeli politicians, Eisenkot sees Iran as an existential threat to Israel and supports military action against the Islamic regime. But he has explicitly warned against escalating the war for political purposes.'Legacy mode'Certainly, Trump may be more willing to attack Iran after the midterms if he is unconstrained electorally and hoping to extract himself from the war with one more push. Some analysts believe Iran is so economically weak from the war and economic sanctions that a fresh round of military strikes might encourage Iranians to overthrow the regime. Others see this as yet more wishful thinking. It is a strategy that has repeatedly failed, but still has currency in Washington."After the midterms, he will be in legacy mode," one well-placed Western diplomat told me. "He will want to show agency on anything that is not the quagmire at home."In Israel there is a broad consensus across most parties about the threat from and the need to constrain Iran. But if voters elect a new government, they might have a prime minister with less political and personal investment in fresh attacks.In those circumstances, Trump has suggested his thinking may change, too. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi [a nickname for Netanyahu], America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote on social media.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Netanyahu has used this year's election campaign to talk up the possibility of a fresh attack on IranLittle wonder policymakers in Tehran have been following US opinion polls as closely as any analyst inside the Washington beltway. The risk, of course, is that any post-electoral strikes would plunge the Middle East into fresh chaos if Iran were to retaliate hard.Publicly and privately, Iranian officials have threatened to hit airports, pipelines, undersea cables, energy facilities, desalination plants as well as US bases and warships.Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, wrote in the Financial Times that new attacks would put "civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk".It's the economyThe two elections again intertwine around the global economy. Affordability and cost of living have dominated campaigning for the midterms, issues made worse by Trump's war that raised prices as Iran choked the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz.The economy is also an election issue in Israel, where voters face high costs and low wages. But here, too, the war plays its part with soaring defence spending putting even more pressure on the public finances.Trump has sought to appease voters ahead of the midterms. He has lifted sanctions on Russia, hoping in vain that by importing diesel from Moscow, prices might fall significantly. He has been taking a tough line with Ukraine, calling on its leadership to make concessions in the hope – also so far in vain – of claiming a foreign policy victory.But Republican ire at his controversial strategy is growing. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a frequent critic of Trump, told CBS News: "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid [favour] for Vladimir Putin."Image source, Chris Torres / EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Early voting has already started in many US states for next month's midtermsOne consequence of the Iran war – along with Israel's military operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank – is that traditional bipartisan support in the US has fractured. Abdul El-Sayed, the left-wing Democratic candidate for the Senate in Michigan, campaigns on cutting military aid to Israel. "An ally that takes your money, to push you into wars you shouldn't be fighting, is not an ally," he told ABC News. The US and Israel initially attacked Iran to destroy its ballistic missiles, degrade its nuclear capability, weaken its support for proxy militias and even oust the entire regime. Since then its war aims have changed to reopening the Strait of Hormuz.Brad Lander, a Democratic congressional candidate in New York who also sits on the left of his party, chose even to travel to the West Bank only days before polling. He helped Palestinians harvest olives and was briefly detained by Israeli forces, all grist to his social media electoral mill. In the history of US politics, this is not normal. Even Netanyahu is warning that Israel may in future have to survive without a US security blanket.Image source, Abir Sultan Credit / EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, The leader of Israel's Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, has ruled out joining a unity government after the electionsOf course, if Israel's prime minister were to lose, his departure would end a scratchy bromance that has seen Trump blow hot and cold. Last week the president called his Israeli counterpart a "great warrior prime minister". During the summer, he said Netanyahu was "effing crazy". A new Israeli leader would have to forge a new relationship with an outgoing US president, a very different dynamic.If the Democrats were to win greater control in Congress, that might place some check on blanket US support for Israel. Congress has traditional powers that it can use to restrain military spending. It could also cut military aid to Israel.  But as president, Trump would retain significant executive power – and a veto – to continue prosecuting the conflict as he saw fit.The decision by Israel and the US to go to war with Iran earlier this year transformed the global economy and international geopolitics. The choices voters in both nations make in coming days may shape where the world goes next.Top image credit: Getty.BBC InDepth is the home on the website and app for the best analysis, with fresh perspectives that challenge assumptions and deep reporting on the biggest issues of the day. Emma Barnett and John Simpson bring their pick of the most thought-provoking deep reads and analysis, every Saturday. title: Why it could take time for a new Israeli government to form
description: Israelis are voting in what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history. It is the first parliamentary election since the
body: Israelis are voting in what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history. It is the first parliamentary election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks and subsequent conflicts across the region - in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen. BBC Middle East correspondent Yolande Knell explains why it may take some time before a new government is formed after the polls close. Read more about the Israel elections.

title: 'A dream come true' - Harry Kane on his Ballon d'Or win
description: Harry Kane has become the first English player to win the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001, after being crowned the world's best player at a cer
body: Harry Kane has become the first English player to win the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001, after being crowned the world's best player at a ceremony in London.Kane scored 61 goals in 51 club matches last season, the most a Bayern Munich player has ever struck in one campaign. He also reached the semi finals of the World Cup with England.Real Madrid and France forward Kylian Mbappe finished second, while Barcelona and Spain attacker Lamine Yamal completed the top three.Read more about how Harry Kane ended England's men's trophy drought.
